Memory Limitations of Prompt Tuning in Transformers

Maxime Meyer Affiliation: Department of Mathematics, National University of Singapore, Singapore, 117543 Affiliation: IPAL, IRL2955, Singapore Email: maxime.meyer@u.nus.edu    Mario Michelessa Affiliation: IPAL, IRL2955, Singapore Affiliation: School of Computing, National University of Singapore, Singapore, 117543 Email: mario.michelessa@u.nus.edu    Caroline Chaux Affiliation: IPAL, IRL2955, Singapore Email: vtan@u.nus.edu    Vincent Y. F. Tan Affiliation: Department of Mathematics, National University of Singapore, Singapore, 117543 Affiliation: Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, National University of Singapore, Singapore, 117543 Email: caroline.chaux@cnrs.fr
Abstract

Despite the empirical success of prompt tuning in adapting pretrained language models to new tasks, theoretical analyses of its capabilities remain limited. Existing theoretical work primarily addresses universal approximation properties, demonstrating results comparable to standard weight tuning. In this paper, we explore a different aspect of the theory of transformers—the memorization capability of prompt tuning—and provide two principal theoretical contributions. First, we prove that the amount of information memorized by a transformer cannot scale faster than linearly with the prompt length. Second, and more importantly, we present the first formal proof of a phenomenon empirically observed in large language models: performance degradation in transformers with extended contexts. We rigorously demonstrate that transformers inherently have limited memory, constraining the amount of information they can retain, regardless of the context size. This finding offers a fundamental understanding of the intrinsic limitations of transformer architectures, particularly their ability to handle long sequences.

1 Introduction

Since their introduction in Vaswani et al. (2017), transformers have reshaped the landscape of machine learning, achieving state-of-the-art results in tasks ranging from natural language processing (Wolf et al., 2020) to computer vision (Dosovitskiy et al., 2021; Zhao et al., 2021; Zhai et al., 2022). A central factor in their success is the ability to adapt pretrained models to downstream tasks via fine-tuning (Howard and Ruder, 2018). Traditionally, this process involves updating the full set of model parameters—a strategy that becomes increasingly costly as models and datasets scale (Brown et al., 2020; Chowdhery et al., 2023).

For large language models (LLMs), prompt tuning has emerged as a parameter-efficient alternative. It enables task adaptation with minimal modification to the model architecture by prepending a small set of learnable parameters (commonly refered as pre-prompt) to the input (e.g. human-readable text for prompt engineering (Chen et al., 2023; Wen et al., 2023) or continuous representations for soft-token optimization (Li and Liang, 2021; Lester et al., 2021)). Despite its simplicity, prompt tuning often matches or exceeds the performance of full fine-tuning, while updating only a small fraction of the model’s parameters (Liu et al., 2022; Wei et al., 2022; Kojima et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2023b; Khattak et al., 2023; Gao et al., 2024; Shi and Lipani, 2024; Fu et al., 2024).

Prompt tuning proves especially effective in settings like in-context learning (Dong et al., 2024), where the pre-prompt includes multiple input/output instances, e.g. “the answer to 𝐗1\mathbf{X}^{1} is 𝐘1\mathbf{Y}^{1}, the answer to 𝐗2\mathbf{X}^{2} is 𝐘2\mathbf{Y}^{2}, …, the answer to 𝐗k\mathbf{X}^{k} is 𝐘k\mathbf{Y}^{k}” for distinct queries 𝐗1,…,𝐗k\mathbf{X}^{1},\dots,\mathbf{X}^{k}. As models scale, one might expect that providing longer pre-prompts should allow a sufficiently large transformer to memorize and generalize from more such examples. However, recent empirical studies suggest that even advanced LLMs struggle to memorize information presented in long prompts (Hsieh et al., 2024; Levy et al., 2024; Laban et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024a; Liu et al., 2024; Jin et al., 2025), despite architectural support (Ding et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024b). In our work, we formally demonstrate and characterize the limited memory not only of current LLMs, but of all transformers when using prompt tuning, by studying the following questions:

Can the pre-prompt length be shortened while retaining information to improve the memorization ability of transformers? Or do transformers have inherent limitations as to the amount of information a pre-prompt can transfer?

We provide the first formal proof of the limited memorization capability of transformers using prompt tuning. Specifically, we prove that there exists an upper bound on the amount of new information a transformer can learn through prompt-tuning, irrespective of pre-prompt length. We further prove that encoding the information in the pre-prompt as input/output pairs is optimal in the sense that the number of distinct items a transformer can memorize via prompt tuning cannot grow faster than linearly with prompt length.

These results reveal fundamental limitations of prompt-based adaptation. Notably, for in-context learning where the pre-prompt consists of a list of kk input/output pairs, one would expect a sufficiently large LLM to be able to memorize this data set—that is to output the correct 𝐘i\mathbf{Y}^{i} when queried with 𝐗i\mathbf{X}^{i}—regardless of kk or the specific values. However, our findings show the opposite. In addition, they imply that the asymptotical gain of soft prompt optimization over prompt engineering is at most linear. This implication complements the main theorem from (Petrov et al., 2024b), which identified a case where soft prompt optimization offers a polynomial gain of order the embedding dimension dd over prompt engineering.

1.1 Contributions

Our contributions can be summarized as follows.

  • •

    We characterize the maximal memorization capability of a transformer with respect to prompt tuning. That is we obtain an integer KK—depending on the parameters of the transformer and on an upper bound RR of the magnitude of tokens—such that for any inputs 𝐗1,…,𝐗k∈ℝd×m\mathbf{X}^{1},...,\mathbf{X}^{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times m}, the proportion of outputs that are accessible through prompt tuning decreases exponentially with kk from the rank k≥Kk\geq K (Section 4.3).

  • •

    We characterize the scaling between the pre-prompt size mpm_{p} and the amount of new information learned by the transformer in Theorem 4.7. More formally, we show that the maximal number kk of input/output pairs of length mm a transformer can reliably learn through prompt tuning of length mpm_{p} scales as k∈O⁡(mpm)k\in O(\frac{m_{p}}{m}) (Section 4.2).

  • •

    We expand on the result from Wang et al. (2023a) and show that, even with no assumptions, a one layer transformer has very little expressivity with regards to prompt tuning. Specifically, we show that the space accessible through prompt tuning for a pair of inputs (𝐗1,𝐗2)(\mathbf{X}^{1},\mathbf{X}^{2}) is almost a hyperplane of the output space. We also generalize this result to approximate memorization, where the goal is to approximate the outputs up to an error ε\varepsilon (Section 5).

  • •

    It is important to note that our first two contributions (Sections 4.2 and 4.3) also hold for masked self-attention. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first work on the approximation theory of prompt tuning to consider this architecture.

1.2 Related Works

Universality of Prompt Tuning. Despite its empirical success, the theoretical understanding of prompt tuning remains limited. Prior work has primarily analyzed its universal approximation properties:

  • •

    Wang et al. (2023a) show that prompt tuning is universal in the sense that for every Lipschitz constant L>0L>0 and error ε\varepsilon, there exists a transformer τ\tau that can approximate any LL-Lipschitz function up to error ε\varepsilon through prompt tuning.

  • •

    Petrov et al. (2024a); Hu et al. (2025) improve this result by further upper bounding the required size of the transformer τ\tau.

  • •

    Nakada et al. (2025) achieve similar results for approximating smooth—rather than Lipschitz—functions.

These studies construct synthetic transformers with weights designed to facilitate prompt tuning. The constructions they use demonstrate approximation power but fail to capture the behavior of pretrained models used in practice. In our work, we depart from this stylized setting by studying the prompt tuning capabilities of an arbitrary transformer.

Comparisons Between Full, Soft Prompt, and Hard Prompt Tuning. The difference between the performances of prompt tuning and full weight fine-tuning was analysed in Oymak et al. (2023); Petrov et al. (2024b). Petrov et al. (2024b) also study the difference between soft prompt tuning and prompt engineering, identifying a setting in which soft prompt tuning is more expressive. Contrary to our work, their analysis is however based on the construction of a specific transformer, and might not hold for any weight attribution.

Memorization Capability of Transformer. There are many works on the memorization capabilities of the transformer architecture. Kim et al. (2023) prove that transformers with 2​n2n self-attention layers suffice for the memorization of length-nn inputs. This result was improved to single-layer transformers in Mahdavi et al. (2024); Kajitsuka and Sato (2024). More recently, Kajitsuka and Sato (2025) study the optimal number of parameters required for memorization.

However, the memorization capability of prompt tuning has been very little studied. The limitations of the memorization capability of a single-layer, single-head transformer satisfying a few assumptions were shown in Wang et al. (2023a). We generalize this setting to any transformer, getting rid of all assumptions. Hu et al. (2025) construct a specific transformer that can memorize datasets. However, this ad hoc transformer is far from the ones being used in practice. Indeed, even for the simple task of memorizing two input/output pairs of size 22, their construction requires a pre-prompt size of length more then 1064010^{640} and more than 101064010^{10^{640}} neurons11 1 Those numbers come directly from Theorem 2.5 of Hu et al. (2025). We considered the ℓ2\ell_{2} norm, with the embedding dimension of BERT-base (Devlin et al., 2019) (d=768d=768), assumed that the input/output pairs (𝐗i,𝐘i)i∈{1,2}(\mathbf{X}^{i},\mathbf{Y}^{i})_{i\in\{1,2\}} are generated by a 11-Lipshitz function (‖𝐘1−𝐘2‖2≤‖𝐗1−𝐗2‖2\|\mathbf{Y}^{1}-\mathbf{Y}^{2}\|_{2}\leq\|\mathbf{X}^{1}-\mathbf{X}^{2}\|_{2}), and aimed for an approximation error of ε=30\varepsilon=30 (generous considering that in practice, this is the order of the maximal norm of an embedded vector in BERT-base (Kobayashi et al., 2020)).—recall that there are “only” about 108010^{80} atoms in the universe.

2 Standard and Mean-Field Transformers

2.1 The Transformer Architecture

We consider transformer networks (Vaswani et al., 2017) composed of repeated self-attention and MLP layers. Let 𝐗∈ℝd×m\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times m} denote the input sequence of mm tokens, each of dimension dd. A single self-attention layer is defined as follows.

Definition 2.1 (Self-Attention Layer).

An hh-head self-attention layer maps every query token 𝐱\mathbf{x} within a context 𝐗∈ℝd×m\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times m} to

Att⁡(𝐱,𝐗)=∑i=1h𝐖oi​𝐖vi​𝐗⋅σ⁡((𝐖ki​𝐗)⊤​𝐖qi​𝐱),\operatorname{Att}(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{X})=\sum_{i=1}^{h}\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{o}}^{i}\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{v}}^{i}\mathbf{X}\cdot\sigma\big((\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{k}}^{i}\mathbf{X})^{\top}\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{q}}^{i}\mathbf{x}\big),

where 𝐖qi,𝐖ki∈ℝs×d,𝐖vi∈ℝs′×d,𝐖oi∈ℝd×s′\mathbf{W}^{i}_{\mathrm{q}},\mathbf{W}^{i}_{\mathrm{k}}\in\mathbb{R}^{s\times d},\mathbf{W}^{i}_{\mathrm{v}}\in\mathbb{R}^{s^{\prime}\times d},\mathbf{W}^{i}_{\mathrm{o}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times s^{\prime}}, ss is called the hidden dimension and is typically taken to be s=s′=dhs=s^{\prime}=\frac{d}{h} (Vaswani et al., 2017; Brown et al., 2020; Dosovitskiy et al., 2021), and the normalization factor 1/s1/\sqrt{s} is absorbed into 𝐖ki\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{k}}^{i} for notational simplicity. The results for each token are then concatenated to produce the output of the self-attention layer

f⁡(𝐗):\displaystyle f(\mathbf{X})\colon =Att⁡(𝐗,𝐗)\displaystyle=\operatorname{Att}(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{X})
=[Att(𝐗:,1,𝐗),…,Att(𝐗:,m,𝐗)].\displaystyle=[\operatorname{Att}(\mathbf{X}_{:,1},\mathbf{X}),\;\ldots,\;\operatorname{Att}(\mathbf{X}_{:,m},\mathbf{X})].

We now define transformer networks, which are a stack of multiple transformer layers composed sequentially.

Definition 2.2 (Transformer Layer).

A transformer layer

ℒ:⋃m=1+∞ℝd×m⟶⋃m=1+∞ℝd×m,\mathcal{L}:\bigcup_{m=1}^{+\infty}\mathbb{R}^{d\times m}\longrightarrow\bigcup_{m=1}^{+\infty}\mathbb{R}^{d\times m},

is defined as

ℒ⁡(𝐗)=MLP⁡(Att⁡(𝐗,𝐗)+𝐗),\mathcal{L}(\mathbf{X})=\operatorname{MLP}\big(\operatorname{Att}(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{X})+\mathbf{X}\big),

with

MLP⁡(𝐗)\displaystyle\operatorname{MLP}(\mathbf{X}) =[𝐖2ReLU(𝐖1𝐗:,1+𝐛1)+𝐛2+𝐗:,1,\displaystyle=\left[\mathbf{W}_{2}\mathrm{ReLU}(\mathbf{W}_{1}\mathbf{X}_{:,1}+\mathbf{b}_{1})+\mathbf{b}_{2}+\mathbf{X}_{:,1},\right.
…,𝐖2ReLU(𝐖1𝐗:,m+𝐛1)+𝐛2+𝐗:,m].\displaystyle\quad\left.\ldots,\mathbf{W}_{2}\mathrm{ReLU}(\mathbf{W}_{1}\mathbf{X}_{:,m}+\mathbf{b}_{1})+\mathbf{b}_{2}+\mathbf{X}_{:,m}\right].

Here, 𝐖1∈ℝdff×d,𝐖2∈ℝd×dff,𝐛1∈ℝdff,𝐛2∈ℝd\mathbf{W}_{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{ff}}\times d},\mathbf{W}_{2}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d_{\mathrm{ff}}},\mathbf{b}_{1}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{ff}}},\mathbf{b}_{2}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, and dffd_{\mathrm{ff}} is the hidden dimension of the MLP.

For simplicity, the layer normalization operation is omitted, following (Kim et al., 2021).

Definition 2.3 (Transformer).

An ll-layer transformer of embedding dimension d∈ℕd\in\mathbb{N}

τ:⋃m=1+∞ℝd×m⟶⋃m=1+∞ℝd×m,\tau:\bigcup_{m=1}^{+\infty}\mathbb{R}^{d\times m}\longrightarrow\bigcup_{m=1}^{+\infty}\mathbb{R}^{d\times m},

is defined as the composition of ll transformer layers

τ=ℒ1∘⋯∘ℒl.\tau=\mathcal{L}_{1}\circ\dots\circ\mathcal{L}_{l}.
Remark 2.4 (On Positional Encodings).

Our definition of the transformer architecture omits positional encodings for clarity of presentation. However, since positional information is typically incorporated via the addition of a fixed or learned matrix to the input sequence, it can be absorbed into the input without affecting the structure of the analysis. As such, all of our results extend immediately to settings where positional encodings are present.

2.2 Mean-Field Transformers

The proof of Theorem 4.10 requires the mean-field generalization of the transformer architecture, as presented in Castin et al. (2024).

When the size of the pre-prompt is large, it can be convenient to interpret a transformer as a map between probability measures rather than finite-length sequences (Sander et al., 2022; Geshkovski et al., 2023). This viewpoint is motivated by the observation that the transformer architecture is permutation equivariant: for any permutation π∈Sn\pi\in S_{n} and any sequence 𝐗∈ℝd×m\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times m}, a transformer τ\tau satisfies

τ⁡(𝐗π⁡(1),…,𝐗π⁡(n))=(τ​(𝐗)π⁡(1),…,τ​(𝐗)π⁡(n)).\tau(\mathbf{X}_{\pi(1)},\ldots,\mathbf{X}_{\pi(n)})=\left(\tau(\mathbf{X})_{\pi(1)},\ldots,\tau(\mathbf{X})_{\pi(n)}\right).

This symmetry motivates replacing the sequence 𝐗\mathbf{X} with its associated empirical measure

M⁡(𝐗):=1m​∑i=1mδ𝐗i,\mathrm{M}(\mathbf{X}):=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\delta_{\mathbf{X}_{i}},

so that a transformer can be viewed as a transformation of probability measures supported on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}, independent of the ordering of tokens. We write 𝒢:=Im⁡(M)={M⁡(𝐗),𝐗∈ℝd×m}\mathcal{G}:=\operatorname{Im}(\mathrm{M})=\{\mathrm{M}(\mathbf{X}),\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times m}\} the image of M\mathrm{M}. To extend the action of transformers beyond empirical measures to general probability distributions, we introduce the notion of pushforward.

Definition 2.5 (Santambrogio (2015)).

Given a probability measure μ\mu on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} and a measurable map φ:ℝd→ℝd\varphi:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R}^{d}, the pushforward of μ\mu by φ\varphi, denoted by φ♯​μ\varphi_{\sharp}\mu, is the probability measure defined on Borel sets B⊂ℝdB\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} by

(φ♯​μ)​(B):=μ⁡(φ−1​(B)).(\varphi_{\sharp}\mu)(B):=\mu(\varphi^{-1}(B)).

Intuitively, φ♯​μ\varphi_{\sharp}\mu is obtained by transporting mass from each point xx to its image φ⁡(x)\varphi(x), preserving total measure. We now define a mean-field transformer.

Definition 2.6 (Mean-Field Self-Attention (Castin et al., 2024)).

The mean-field generalization FF of any self-attention layer—parameterized by projection matrices 𝐖q\mathbf{W}_{q}, 𝐖k\mathbf{W}_{k}, 𝐖v\mathbf{W}_{v}, and 𝐖o\mathbf{W}_{o} as defined in Definition 2.1—is defined by

F:μ∈𝒫c​(ℝd)↦(Γμ)♯​μ∈𝒫c​(ℝd),whereF:\mu\in\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{c}}(\mathbb{R}^{d})\mapsto(\Gamma_{\mu})_{\sharp}\mu\in\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{c}}(\mathbb{R}^{d}),\quad\mbox{where}
Γμ​(𝐱):=∑i=1h∫𝐖oi​𝐖vi​𝐲⋅exp⁡((𝐖ki​𝐲)⊤​𝐖qi​𝐱)​𝑑μ​(𝐲)∫exp⁡((𝐖ki​𝐲)⊤​𝐖qi​𝐱)​𝑑μ​(𝐲),\Gamma_{\mu}(\mathbf{x}):=\sum_{i=1}^{h}\frac{\int\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{o}}^{i}\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{v}}^{i}\mathbf{y}\cdot\exp\big((\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{k}}^{i}\mathbf{y})^{\top}\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{q}}^{i}\mathbf{x}\big)\,\mathrm{d}\mu(\mathbf{y})}{\int\exp\big((\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{k}}^{i}\mathbf{y})^{\top}\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{q}}^{i}\mathbf{x}\big)\,\mathrm{d}\mu(\mathbf{y})},

Mean-field self-attention FF generalizes discrete self-attention Att\operatorname{Att} in the sense that for any input 𝐗∈ℝd×m\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times m}, we have F⁡(M⁡(𝐗))=M⁡(Att⁡(𝐗,𝐗))F(\mathrm{M}(\mathbf{X}))=\mathrm{M}(\operatorname{Att}(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{X})).

Definition 2.7 (Mean-Field Transformer Layer).

Similarly, any transformer layer τ\tau, with MLP layer MLP\operatorname{MLP} and mean-field self-attention layer defined by Γ⋅\Gamma_{\cdot}, has the following mean-field generalization TT.

T:μ∈𝒫c​(ℝd)↦(Δμ)♯​μ∈𝒫c​(ℝd),whereT:\mu\in\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{c}}(\mathbb{R}^{d})\mapsto(\Delta_{\mu})_{\sharp}\mu\in\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{c}}(\mathbb{R}^{d}),\quad\mbox{where}
Δμ​(𝐱):=MLP⁡(Γμ​(𝐱)+𝐱).\Delta_{\mu}(\mathbf{x}):=\operatorname{MLP}(\Gamma_{\mu}(\mathbf{x})+\mathbf{x}).

Similarly to mean-field self-attention, we prove in Appendix A that a mean-field transformer layer TT generalizes a discrete transformer layer τ\tau in the sense that for any input 𝐗∈ℝd×m\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times m}, we have T⁡(M⁡(𝐗))=M⁡(τ⁡(𝐗))T(\mathrm{M}(\mathbf{X}))=\mathrm{M}(\tau(\mathbf{X})).

The study of the mean-field framework requires the introduction of a distance on the set of compactly supported probability measures on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. This motivates the following definition.

Definition 2.8 (qq-Wasserstein Distance (Santambrogio, 2015)).

For q≥1q\geq 1, the LqL_{q} Wasserstein distance on 𝒫c​(ℝd)\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{c}}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) is given by

Wq​(μ,ν):=(infπ∈Π⁡(μ,ν)∫‖x−y‖q​𝑑π​(x,y))1/q,W_{q}(\mu,\nu):=\left(\inf_{\pi\in\Pi(\mu,\nu)}\int\|x-y\|^{q}\,\mathrm{d}\pi(x,y)\right)^{1/q},

for μ,ν∈𝒫c​(ℝd)\mu,\nu\in\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{c}}(\mathbb{R}^{d}), where Π⁡(μ,ν)\Pi(\mu,\nu) is the set of couplings between μ\mu and ν\nu, i.e. of probability measures π∈𝒫⁡(ℝd×ℝd)\pi\in\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}) such that ∫π⁡(⋅,y)​𝑑y=μ\int\pi(\cdot,y)\,\mathrm{d}y=\mu and ∫π⁡(x,⋅)​𝑑x=ν\int\pi(x,\cdot)\,\mathrm{d}x=\nu.

2.3 The Lipschitz Constant of Transformers

One of the main property of transformers and their mean-field generalizations that we use in this study is that they are Lipschitz.

Definition 2.9 (Lipschitz).

A function f:E⟶Ff:E\longrightarrow F is said to be LL-Lipschitz for some L>0L>0 with regards to a distance dd if

∀x,y∈E,d⁡(f⁡(x),f⁡(y))≤L​d​(x,y).\forall x,y\in E,d\big(f(x),f(y)\big)\leq Ld(x,y).
Remark 2.10.

Recall that to every norm ∥⋅∥\|\cdot\| is associated the distance

d⁡(x,y)=‖x−y‖.d(x,y)=\|x-y\|.

Unbounded Setting.

Without bounding the input in a ball of radius rr, self-attention (and therefore a transformer) is not globally Lipschitz. In particular, Kim et al. (2021) show that the Lipschitz constant becomes unbounded as the norm of the inputs diverges. Consequently, all existing upper bounds require restricting the input sequences to a bounded subset of ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. This is not a significant limitation in practice, since the input space is finite and therefore necessarily bounded.

Lipschitz Properties of Self-Attention.

The value of the Lipschitz constant for standard single-head self-attention has been rigorously analyzed by Castin et al. (2024), who establish both upper and lower bounds in the finite-token regime, when considering the Frobenius norm ∥⋅∥F\|\cdot\|_{\mathrm{F}}. The bounds are stated using the operator norm induced by ∥⋅∥F\|\cdot\|_{\mathrm{F}}, which we will denote ∥⋅∥op\|\cdot\|_{\mathrm{op}}.

Proposition 2.11 (Castin et al. (2024)).

When inputs lie in a compact ball of radius rr, single-head self-attention with parameters (𝐀=𝐖k⊤​𝐖q,𝐖v)(\mathbf{A}=\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{k}}^{\top}\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{q}},\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{v}}) is Lipschitz continuous, with constant bounded by

Lip∥⋅∥F(f|Bn​(0,r))≤3∥𝐖v∥op‖𝐀‖op2​r4​(4​n+1)+n.\operatorname{Lip}^{\|\cdot\|_{\mathrm{F}}}\left(f|_{B^{n}(0,r)}\right)\leq\sqrt{3}\|\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{v}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\sqrt{\|\mathbf{A}\|_{\mathrm{op}}^{2}r^{4}(4n+1)+n}.

This estimate captures the n\sqrt{n} growth of sensitivity with respect to the sequence length. This growth rate is tight for moderate nn, specifically when

n≤1+exp⁡(2​r2​γ),where\displaystyle n\leq 1+\exp(2r^{2}\gamma),\quad\mbox{where}
γ=max⁡(−γmin,γmax8),\displaystyle\gamma=\max(-\gamma_{\mathrm{min}},\frac{\gamma_{\mathrm{max}}}{8}),

with γmin\gamma_{\mathrm{min}} and γmax\gamma_{\mathrm{max}} the minimal and maximal real eigenvalues of 𝐀\mathbf{A} respectively.

Mean-Field Regime.

As the sequence length nn increases, the bound above becomes loose, eventually diverging as n→∞n\to\infty with fixed radius rr. The mean-field regime allows to overcome this limitation.

Proposition 2.12 (Geshkovski et al. (2023)).

When inputs lie in a compact ball of radius rr, mean-field single-head self-attention with parameters (𝐀=𝐖k⊤​𝐖q,𝐖v)(\mathbf{A}=\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{k}}^{\top}\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{q}},\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{v}}) is Lipschitz continuous, with constant bounded by

LipW2⁡(F|𝒫​(Bn​(0,r)))≤‖𝐖v‖op​(1CLOSE\displaystyle\operatorname{Lip}^{W_{2}}\left(F|_{\mathcal{P}(B^{n}(0,r))}\right)\leq\|\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{v}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}(1 OPEN+3​‖𝐀‖op​r2)​exp⁡(2​‖𝐀‖op​r2).\displaystyle+3\|\mathbf{A}\|_{\mathrm{op}}r^{2})\exp\left(2\|\mathbf{A}\|_{\mathrm{op}}r^{2}\right).
Remark 2.13 (Castin et al. (2024)).

Let r>0r>0. Then,

Lip∥⋅∥F(f|Bn​(0,r))≤LipW2(F|𝒫​(Bn​(0,r))).\operatorname{Lip}^{\|\cdot\|_{\mathrm{F}}}\left(f\big|_{B^{n}(0,r)}\right)\leq\operatorname{Lip}^{W_{2}}\left(F\big|_{\mathcal{P}(B^{n}(0,r))}\right).

This inequality illustrates that the Lipschitz constant of the mean-field self-attention map upper bounds that of its finite-token counterpart, thereby connecting the two frameworks.

2.4 Masked Self-Attention

While most existing theoretical work on transformers—including all prior analyses of prompt tuning cited in this paper—focuses on unmasked self-attention, this framework does not capture the architecture of decoder-only models (Liu et al., 2018; OpenAI et al., 2024). These models employ masked self-attention, in which each token attends only to its past, inducing a sequential structure. In this work, we incorporate masked self-attention into our analysis.

Definition 2.14.

Given a self-attention operator f⁡(𝐗)=Att⁡(𝐗,𝐗)f(\mathbf{X})=\operatorname{Att}(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{X}) (as in Definition 2.1), we define masked self-attention as the map

fm:⋃m∈ℕℝd×m→⋃m∈ℕℝd×m,such that\displaystyle f^{\mathrm{m}}\colon\bigcup_{m\in\mathbb{N}}\mathbb{R}^{d\times m}\to\bigcup_{m\in\mathbb{N}}\mathbb{R}^{d\times m},\quad\mbox{such that}
fm​(𝐗)i:=f​([𝐗1,…,𝐗i])ifor ​𝐗∈ℝd×m.\displaystyle f^{m}(\mathbf{X})_{i}:=f([\mathbf{X}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{X}_{i}])_{i}\quad\text{for }\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times m}.

Proposition 2.11 still holds for masked self-attention.

Proposition 2.15 (Castin et al. (2024)).

When inputs lie in a compact ball of radius rr, single-head masked self-attention with parameters (𝐀=𝐖k⊤​𝐖q,𝐖v)(\mathbf{A}=\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{k}}^{\top}\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{q}},\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{v}}) is Lipschitz continuous, with constant bounded by

Lip∥⋅∥F(fm|Bn​(0,r))≤3∥\displaystyle\operatorname{Lip}^{\|\cdot\|_{\mathrm{F}}}\left(f^{\mathrm{m}}|_{B^{n}(0,r)}\right)\leq\sqrt{3}\| 𝐖v∥op‖𝐀‖op2​r4​(4​n+1)+n.\displaystyle\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{v}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}\sqrt{\|\mathbf{A}\|_{\mathrm{op}}^{2}r^{4}(4n+1)+n}.

Since masked self-attention is not permutation invariant, it is not as straightforward to extend fmf^{\mathrm{m}} in the mean-field regime. The trick is to extend the input space to [0,1]×ℝd[0,1]\times\mathbb{R}^{d}, allowing each token to carry a timestamp representing its location in the sequence.

Position-Aware Distance for Masked Self-Attention

To study the Lipschitz regularity of masked self-attention, the standard Wasserstein distance is not suitable. Indeed, mean-field masked self-attention operates on inputs of the form (s,𝐱)∈[0,1]×ℝd(s,\mathbf{x})\in[0,1]\times\mathbb{R}^{d}, where the extra coordinate ss encodes the position in the sequence. The Wasserstein distance, however, allows moving mass between points with different positions s≠s′s\neq s^{\prime}, which breaks the sequential structure of masked attention. To fix this, Castin et al. (2024) introduce a new distance on 𝒫c​([0,1]×ℝd)\mathcal{P}_{c}([0,1]\times\mathbb{R}^{d}) that only compares points with the same position. With this new distance dmd^{\mathrm{m}}, the Lipschitz constant of mean-field masked self-attention has the same upper bound as its unmasked counterpart.

Proposition 2.16 (Geshkovski et al. (2023)).

When inputs lie in a compact ball of radius rr, mean-field single-head masked self-attention with parameters (𝐀=𝐖k⊤​𝐖q,𝐖v)(\mathbf{A}=\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{k}}^{\top}\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{q}},\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{v}}) is Lipschitz continuous, with constant bounded by

Lipdm⁡(Fm|𝒫​(Bn​(0,r)))≤‖𝐖v‖op​(1CLOSE\displaystyle\operatorname{Lip}^{d^{\mathrm{m}}}\left(F^{\mathrm{m}}|_{\mathcal{P}(B^{n}(0,r))}\right)\leq\|\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{v}}\|_{\mathrm{op}}(1 OPEN+3​‖𝐀‖op​r2)​exp⁡(2​‖𝐀‖op​r2).\displaystyle+3\|\mathbf{A}\|_{\mathrm{op}}r^{2})\exp\left(2\|\mathbf{A}\|_{\mathrm{op}}r^{2}\right).

3 Covering and Packing Numbers

Our proofs require the notions of covering and packing numbers (Vershynin, 2025).

Definition 3.1 (Covering Number).

Let (T,d)(T,d) be a metric space and let ε>0\varepsilon>0.

The ε\varepsilon-covering number of TT, denoted 𝒩⁡(T,d,ε)\mathcal{N}(T,d,\varepsilon), is the minimal number of balls of radius ε\varepsilon (with respect to the metric dd) needed to cover TT. That is,

𝒩(T,d,ε)=min{N∈ℕ,∃(xi)i∈[N]∈TN,T⊂⋃i=1NB(xi,ε)}.\displaystyle\mathcal{N}(T,d,\varepsilon)=\min\{N\in\mathbb{N},\kern 5.0pt\exists(x_{i})_{i\in[N]}\in T^{N},\kern 5.0ptT\subset\bigcup_{i=1}^{N}B(x_{i},\varepsilon)\}.
Definition 3.2 (Packing Number).

Let (T,d)(T,d) be a metric space and let ε>0\varepsilon>0.

The ε\varepsilon-packing number of TT, denoted ℳ⁡(T,d,ε)\mathcal{M}(T,d,\varepsilon), is the maximal number of disjoint open balls of radius ε2\frac{\varepsilon}{2} that can be placed in TT, or equivalently, the largest cardinality of an ε\varepsilon-separated subset of TT. That is,

ℳ(T,d,ε)=max{M∈ℕ,∃(xi)i∈[M]∈TM,∀i≠j,d(xi,xj)>ε}.\displaystyle\mathcal{M}(T,d,\varepsilon)=\max\{M\in\mathbb{N},\kern 5.0pt\exists(x_{i})_{i\in[M]}\in T^{M},\kern 5.0pt\forall i\neq j,d(x_{i},x_{j})>\varepsilon\}.

Notice that the covering and packing numbers are essentially equivalent:

Lemma 3.3 (Approximate Equivalence of Covering and Packing Numbers (Vershynin, 2025, Lemma 4.2.8)).

For any set K⊂TK\subset T and any ε>0\varepsilon>0, we have

𝒫⁡(K,d,2​ε)≤𝒩⁡(K,d,ε)≤𝒫⁡(K,d,ε).\mathcal{P}(K,d,2\varepsilon)\leq\mathcal{N}(K,d,\varepsilon)\leq\mathcal{P}(K,d,\varepsilon).

We use the following main result to analyze the setting of bounded length prompts (Section 4.2).

Proposition 3.4 (Vershynin (2025, Proposition 4.2.10)).

Let n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N}, K⊂ℝnK\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} and ε>0\varepsilon>0. Then,

Vol⁡(K)Vol⁡(ε​Bn​(0,1))≤𝒩(K,∥⋅∥,ε),and\displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{Vol}(K)}{\mathrm{Vol}(\varepsilon B^{n}(0,1))}\ \leq\ \mathcal{N}(K,\|\cdot\|,\varepsilon),\quad\mbox{and}
𝒫(K,∥⋅∥,ε)≤Vol⁡(K+(ε/2)​Bn​(0,1))Vol⁡((ε/2)​Bn​(0,1)).\displaystyle\ \ \mathcal{P}(K,\|\cdot\|,\varepsilon)\ \leq\ \frac{\mathrm{Vol}(K+(\varepsilon/2)B^{n}(0,1))}{\mathrm{Vol}((\varepsilon/2)B^{n}(0,1))}.

The mean-field framework

We obtain similar results for the study of prompts of arbitrary length in the mean-field framework (Section 4.3).

Proposition 3.5 (Nguyen (2013, Lemma 4.b)).

Let 𝒢\mathcal{G} be the set of discrete probability measures on the token embeddings of dimension dd as defined in Section 2.2. Then for any q≥1,ε>0q\geq 1,\varepsilon>0,

logN(𝒢,Wq,2ε)≤N(Θ,∥⋅∥,ε)log(e+e​Diam​(Θ)qεq),\log N(\mathcal{G},W_{q},2\varepsilon)\leq N(\Theta,\|\cdot\|,\varepsilon)\log\Big(e+\frac{e\,\mathrm{Diam}(\Theta)^{q}}{\varepsilon^{q}}\Big),

with Θ=Bd​(0,r)\Theta=B^{d}(0,r) and e=exp⁡(1)e=\exp(1).

Proposition 3.6.

Let 𝒢\mathcal{G} be the set of discrete probability measures on the token embeddings of dimension dd as defined in Section 2.2. Then for any q≥1,ε>0q\geq 1,\varepsilon>0, there exists C>0C>0 such that

𝒩⁡(𝒢,Wq,ε)≥1C​exp⁡(1εd).\mathcal{N}(\mathcal{G},W_{q},\varepsilon)\geq\frac{1}{C}\exp(\frac{1}{\varepsilon^{d}}).

We prove this result in Appendix B.

4 The Limited Memorization Capability of Transformers

In this section, we formally demonstrate the limitations of transformers for long prompt memorization. We introduce a few useful definitions in Section 4.1. In Section 4.2 we prove that the amount of information memorized by a transformer from a prompt scales at most linearly with the prompt length. We then show in Section 4.3 that, since the amount of information a transformer can memorize through prompt tuning is limited, the first result translates directly to an incapacity of memorizing long prompts.

4.1 Accessible Outputs

It is useful to introduce a few definitions for the statement and proofs of our main results.

Accessible Output Sequences

Definition 4.1 (ε\varepsilon-Distinct Vector Sequences).

Two vector sequences 𝐘=(𝐘i)i∈[k],𝐙=(𝐙i)i∈[k]∈(Rd)k\mathbf{Y}=(\mathbf{Y}^{i})_{i\in[k]},\mathbf{Z}=(\mathbf{Z}^{i})_{i\in[k]}\in\mathbb{(}R^{d})^{k} are said to be ε\varepsilon-distinct under norm ∥⋅∥\|\cdot\| if

there exists an ​i∈[k]​ such that ​‖𝐘i−𝐙i‖>ε.\text{there exists an }i\in[k]\text{ such that }\|\mathbf{Y}^{i}-\mathbf{Z}^{i}\|>\varepsilon.

Several vector sequences are said to be ε\varepsilon-distinct under norm ∥⋅∥\|\cdot\| if they are pairwise ε\varepsilon-distinct under norm ∥⋅∥\|\cdot\|. We use the notion of output sequence (respectively input sequences) when the vectors considered are the outputs (respectively inputs) vector sequences of a transformer.

Definition 4.2 (ε\varepsilon-Accessible Output Sequence).

For a fixed transformer τ\tau, a pre-prompt 𝐏∈ℝd×mp\mathbf{P}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times m_{p}} is said to approximate an output sequence 𝐘=(𝐘i)i∈[k]∈(Rd×m)k\mathbf{Y}=(\mathbf{Y}^{i})_{i\in[k]}\in\mathbb{(}R^{d\times m})^{k} under norm ∥⋅∥\|\cdot\| up to error ε\varepsilon for an input sequence 𝐗=(𝐗i)i∈[k]∈(Rd×m)k\mathbf{X}=(\mathbf{X}^{i})_{i\in[k]}\in\mathbb{(}R^{d\times m})^{k} if

∀i∈[k],∥τ([𝐏,𝐗i]):,mp:−𝐘i∥≤ε.\forall i\in[k],\quad\|\tau([\mathbf{P},\mathbf{X}^{i}])_{:,m_{p}:}-\mathbf{Y}^{i}\|\leq\varepsilon. (1)

An output sequence 𝐘\mathbf{Y} is said to be ε\varepsilon-accessible under norm ∥⋅∥\|\cdot\| by an input sequence 𝐗\mathbf{X} if there exists a pre-prompt 𝐏\mathbf{P} that approximates 𝐘\mathbf{Y} for 𝐗\mathbf{X} under norm ∥⋅∥\|\cdot\| up to error ε\varepsilon.

Remark 4.3.

Historically, theoretical work on prompt tuning removes the first part of the output, corresponding to the pre-prompt, in the approximation objective (Equation (1)). That is the goal is to find a pre-prompt 𝐏∈ℝd×mp\mathbf{P}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times m_{p}} such that the last part of the output τ([𝐏,𝐗i]):,mp:\tau([\mathbf{P},\mathbf{X}^{i}])_{:,m_{p}:} approximates 𝐘\mathbf{Y}.

Accessible Output Distributions

We can adapt the notion of accessible outputs to the mean-field framework.

Definition 4.4 (ε\varepsilon-Distinct Vector Distributions).

Two vector distributions μY,μZ∈𝒫c​(ℝd)\mu_{Y},\mu_{Z}\in\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{c}}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) are said to be ε\varepsilon-distinct under distance WqW_{q} for some q≥1q\geq 1 if

Wq​(μY,μZ)>ε.W_{q}(\mu_{Y},\mu_{Z})>\varepsilon.

Several vector distributions are said to be ε\varepsilon-distinct under distance WqW_{q} if they are pairwise ε\varepsilon-distinct under distance WqW_{q}. We use the notion of output distributions when the considered vectors are the output distributions of a transformer.

Definition 4.5 (ε\varepsilon-Accessible Output Distribution).

For a fixed transformer τ\tau with mean-field generalization TT, a pre-prompt 𝐏∈ℝd×mp\mathbf{P}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times m_{p}} is said to approximate an output distribution μY∈𝒫c​(ℝd)\mu_{Y}\in\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{c}}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) under distance WqW_{q} up to error ε\varepsilon for an input sequence 𝐗∈(Rd×m)k\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{(}R^{d\times m})^{k} if Wq​(T⁡(M⁡([𝐏,𝐗i])),μY)≤εW_{q}\Big(T\big(M([\mathbf{P},\mathbf{X}^{i}])\big),\mu_{Y}\Big)\leq\varepsilon. An output distribution μY\mu_{Y} is said to be ε\varepsilon-accessible by an input sequence 𝐗\mathbf{X} if there exists mp∈ℕm_{p}\in\mathbb{N} and a pre-prompt of length mpm_{p}, 𝐏∈ℝd×mp\mathbf{P}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times m_{p}} that approximates μY\mu_{Y} under distance WqW_{q} for 𝐗\mathbf{X} up to error ε\varepsilon.

Remark 4.6.

In contrast to Remark 4.3, our mean-field formulation does not discard the portion of the transformer’s output corresponding to the pre-prompt. Instead, the output is modeled as a full probability distribution over token embeddings, which naturally incorporates the pre-prompt part of the output. Nevertheless, by leveraging positional encodings, one can still enforce constraints specifically on the final part of the output, thereby recovering the standard approximation objective.

4.2 The Limit on the Amount of Information that Can Be Contained in A Prompt

Let us show that the maximal number kk of input/output pairs of length mm a transformer can reliably learn through prompt tuning of length mpm_{p} scales as k∈O⁡(mpm)k\in O(\frac{m_{p}}{m}).

Theorem 4.7.

Let τ\tau be a transformer of Lipschitz constant LL, embedding radius rr and embedding dimension dd. Then, for k>mp​log⁡(3​L​r)−log⁡(ε)log⁡(r)−log⁡(3​ε)k>m_{p}\frac{\log(3Lr)-\log(\varepsilon)}{\log(r)-\log(3\varepsilon)} and any list of kk inputs of size mm, 𝐗=(𝐗1,…,𝐗k)∈(ℝd×m)k\mathbf{X}=(\mathbf{X}^{1},\dots,\mathbf{X}^{k})\in(\mathbb{R}^{d\times m})^{k}, the proportion (in terms of volume) of output sequences that are ε\varepsilon-accessible is at most [(3​L​rε)mp(r3​ε)m​k]d∈O⁡((r3​ε)−m​d​k)\Big[\frac{(\frac{3Lr}{\varepsilon})^{m_{p}}}{(\frac{r}{3\varepsilon})^{mk}}\Big]^{d}\in O((\frac{r}{3\varepsilon})^{-mdk}).

That is the proportion of output sequences that are ε\varepsilon-accessible through prompt tuning decreases exponentially fast with k≥C​mpmk\geq C\frac{m_{p}}{m}, where CC is a function of the parameters of the transformer and of the target precision ε\varepsilon.

Remark 4.8.

Theorem 4.7 still holds when considering masked self-attention.

Sketch of Proof.

Our proof can be divided into three steps:

  • •

    We obtain a number Cout​(m​k)C_{\mathrm{out}}(mk) of 3​ε3\varepsilon-distinct output sequences.

  • •

    We prove—by discretizing the pre-prompt space and using the Lipschitz property of τ\tau—that there exists a maximal number CinC_{\mathrm{in}} of those output sequences that are ε\varepsilon-accessible.

  • •

    If Cout​(m​k)>CinC_{\mathrm{out}}(mk)>C_{\mathrm{in}}, then the proportion of ε\varepsilon-accessible output sequences is at most CinCout\frac{C_{\mathrm{in}}}{C_{\mathrm{out}}}.

The formulas for CinC_{\mathrm{in}} and CoutC_{\mathrm{out}} are obtained using the notions of covering and packing numbers (Section 3). ∎

The full proof can be found in Appendix C.

Remark 4.9.

Note that Theorem 4.7 requires r>3​εr>3\varepsilon for the proof to hold. However, this is a natural assumption as the problem becomes trivial if the target precision ε\varepsilon is of the same order as the maximal norm rr of the vectors that are to be approximated.

4.3 The Limit on the Amount of Information a Transformer can Memorize through Prompt Tuning

Building on the mean-field framework defined in Section 2.2, we prove that the memorization capability of transformers is limited, independantly of prompt size.

Theorem 4.10.

Let τ\tau be a transformer with mean-field generalization TT of Lipschitz constant LL, embedding radius rr and embedding dimension dd. Then for k>(6​L​rε)d​(1+log⁡(1+(4​L​rε)q))(3ε)d−log⁡(C)k>\frac{(\frac{6Lr}{\varepsilon})^{d}(1+\log(1+(\frac{4Lr}{\varepsilon})^{q}))}{(\frac{3}{\varepsilon})^{d}-\log(C)} and any list of kk inputs of size mm, 𝐗=(𝐗1,…,𝐗k)∈(ℝd×m)k\mathbf{X}=(\mathbf{X}^{1},\dots,\mathbf{X}^{k})\in(\mathbb{R}^{d\times m})^{k}, the proportion of output distributions that are ε\varepsilon-accessible is at most (e⁡(1+(4​L​rε)q))(6​L​rε)d(1C​exp⁡(3dεd))k∈O⁡(exp⁡(−k​3dεd))\frac{\Big(e\big(1+(\frac{4Lr}{\varepsilon})^{q}\big)\Big)^{(\frac{6Lr}{\varepsilon})^{d}}}{\big(\frac{1}{C}\exp(\frac{3^{d}}{\varepsilon^{d}})\big)^{k}}\in O\big(\exp(-k\frac{3^{d}}{\varepsilon^{d}})\big).

That is the proportion of output distributions that are ε\varepsilon-accessible through prompt tuning decreases exponentially fast for large enough kk.

Remark 4.11.

It is straightforward to extend Theorem 4.10 to masked self-attention.

Sketch of Proof.

The proof follows the same sketch as for Theorem 4.7, and the full version can be found in Appendix D. ∎

5 The Limitations of Prompt Tuning on Single-Layer Transformers

5.1 Existing Results

The only current theoretical result on the limitations of the expressivity of prompt tuning in transformers is the following, which relies on a few assumptions.

Assumption 5.1.
  • •

    𝐖q,𝐖k,𝐖v\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{q}},\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{k}},\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{v}} are full rank.

  • •

    Att⁡(𝐗i,𝐗i)+𝐗i\operatorname{Att}(\mathbf{X}^{i},\mathbf{X}^{i})+\mathbf{X}^{i} are distinct.

  • •

    (𝐘i)i,k(\mathbf{Y}^{i})_{i,k} are in the range set of MLP\operatorname{MLP}.

Assumption 5.2.

d⩾2+dim[(MLP−1((𝐲10)−𝐱0)∪(MLP−1(𝐲20)−𝐱0)]d\geqslant 2+\operatorname{dim}[(\operatorname{MLP}^{-1}((\mathbf{y}_{10})-\mathbf{x}_{0})\cup(\operatorname{MLP}^{-1}(\mathbf{y}_{20})-\mathbf{x}_{0})]. This condition is satisfied as long as

‖𝐖1‖2⋅‖𝐖2‖2<1,\|\mathbf{W}_{1}\|_{2}\cdot\|\mathbf{W}_{2}\|_{2}<1,

where ∥⋅∥2\|\cdot\|_{2} denotes the matrix spectral norm.

Assumption 5.3.
  • •

    There is only one head: h=1h=1.

  • •

    The symmetric part (𝐖q⊤​𝐖k)+(𝐖q⊤​𝐖k)⊤2\frac{(\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{q}}^{\top}\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{k}})+(\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{q}}^{\top}\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{k}})^{\top}}{2} of 𝐖q⊤​𝐖k\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{q}}^{\top}\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{k}} has full rank.

Notice that Assumption 5.1 is especially strong as 𝐖v\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{v}} is typically of rank s=dh≪ds=\frac{d}{h}\ll d (s=64,d=768,h=12s=64,d=768,h=12 and there are 1212 attention layers for BERT-Base (Devlin et al., 2019)).

Theorem 5.4 (Wang et al. (2023a)).

For a single-layer transformer τ\tau satisfying Assumptions 5.1, 5.2, and 5.3, there exist (𝐗1,𝐘1)(\mathbf{X}^{1},\mathbf{Y}^{1}), (𝐗2,𝐘2)(\mathbf{X}^{2},\mathbf{Y}^{2}) such that ∀mp∈ℕ,∀𝐏∈ℝd×mp,τ⁡([𝐏,𝐗i])≠𝐘i\forall m_{p}\in\mathbb{N},\forall\mathbf{P}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times m_{p}},\tau([\mathbf{P},\mathbf{X}^{i}])\neq\mathbf{Y}^{i} for some i∈{1,2}i\in\{1,2\}.

5.2 Generalization to weaker assumptions and several heads

We first show that we can generalize Theorem 5.4 by keeping only the mild following assumption.

Assumption 5.5.
‖𝐖1‖2⋅‖𝐖2‖2<1,\|\mathbf{W}_{1}\|_{2}\cdot\|\mathbf{W}_{2}\|_{2}<1,

where ∥⋅∥2\|\cdot\|_{2} denotes the matrix spectral norm.

Remark 5.6.

Experimental results in (Dong et al., 2021) indicate that, for most architectures, the weight matrices have small operator norms. Consequently, the condition ‖𝐖1‖2⋅‖𝐖2‖2<1\|\mathbf{W}_{1}\|_{2}\cdot\|\mathbf{W}_{2}\|_{2}<1 is mild and typically satisfied in practice.

We prove the stronger result that prompt tuning on a single-layer transformer has very little expressiveness in terms of dimensions. That is the transformer cannot memorize most pairs (𝐗1,𝐘1),(𝐗2,𝐘2)(\mathbf{X}^{1},\mathbf{Y}^{1}),(\mathbf{X}^{2},\mathbf{Y}^{2}) such that 𝐗1\mathbf{X}^{1} and 𝐗2\mathbf{X}^{2} share at least one common token.

Theorem 5.7.

Let τ\tau be a 1-layer transformer with hh heads such that d−h2−2​h>0d-h^{2}-2h>0. Then ∀𝐱0,𝐱1,𝐱2∈ℝd\forall\mathbf{x}_{0},\mathbf{x}_{1},\mathbf{x}_{2}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, there exists an ℝ\mathbb{R}-vector space EE of dimension (d−h2−h)!(d−h2−2​h−1)!\frac{(d-h^{2}-h)!}{(d-h^{2}-2h-1)!} such that ∀(𝐲1,…,𝐲h+1)∈MLP⁡(E∖{0}),\forall(\mathbf{y}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{y}_{h+1})\in\operatorname{MLP}(E\setminus\{0\}), ∀mp∈ℕ,∀𝐏∈ℝd×mP,τ​([𝐏,𝐱i,𝐱0])−1≠𝐲i\forall m_{p}\in\mathbb{N},\forall\mathbf{P}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times m_{P}},\tau([\mathbf{P},\mathbf{x}_{i},\mathbf{x}_{0}])_{-1}\neq\mathbf{y}_{i} for some i∈{1,2}i\in\{1,2\}.

In other words, "the space accessible through prompt tuning on a single layer is more or less a hyperplane of the space of all available outputs".

Sketch of Proof.

The proof of Theorem 5.7 is based on the fact that the single-head attention of (𝐱0,[𝐏,𝐱i,𝐱0])(\mathbf{x}_{0},[\mathbf{P},\mathbf{x}^{i},\mathbf{x}^{0}]) can be decomposed as a part depending only on (𝐱0,𝐏)(\mathbf{x}^{0},\mathbf{P}), and a part depending only of (𝐱0,𝐱i)(\mathbf{x}^{0},\mathbf{x}^{i}),

Att⁡(𝐱0,[𝐏,𝐱i,𝐱0])=𝐚0𝐏+𝐚i.\operatorname{Att}(\mathbf{x}_{0},[\mathbf{P},\mathbf{x}^{i},\mathbf{x}^{0}])=\mathbf{a}_{0}^{\mathbf{P}}+\mathbf{a}_{i}.

So we can see single-head single-layer attention as modifying the last vector of all inputs 𝐗i\mathbf{X}^{i} along a same axis 𝐚i\mathbf{a}_{i}. If the number of independant contraints (in our case the number of outputs 𝐲i\mathbf{y}_{i}) becomes higher than the number of parameters, then the output becomes unaccessible. ∎

The proof of Theorem 5.7 can be found in Appendix E.

5.3 Generalization to approximate memorization

We show that prompt tuning on a single-layer transformer won’t work even when the goal is relaxed to only learning an approximation of the output 𝐘i\mathbf{Y}^{i}.

Theorem 5.8.

Let τ\tau be a 1-layer transformer with hh heads such that d−h2−2​h>0d-h^{2}-2h>0. Then ∀𝐱0,𝐱1,𝐱2∈ℝd\forall\mathbf{x}_{0},\mathbf{x}_{1},\mathbf{x}_{2}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, there exists an ℝ\mathbb{R}-vector space EE of dimension (d−h2−h)!(d−h2−2​h−1)!\frac{(d-h^{2}-h)!}{(d-h^{2}-2h-1)!} such that ∀(𝐲1,…,𝐲h+1)∈MLP⁡(E∖{0}),\forall(\mathbf{y}_{1},\dots,\mathbf{y}_{h+1})\in\operatorname{MLP}(E\setminus\{0\}), ∀mp∈ℕ,∀𝐏∈ℝd×mP,τ​([𝐏,𝐱i,𝐱0])−1≥(1−‖𝐖1‖2⋅‖𝐖2‖2)​r2\forall m_{p}\in\mathbb{N},\forall\mathbf{P}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times m_{P}},\tau([\mathbf{P},\mathbf{x}_{i},\mathbf{x}_{0}])_{-1}\geq\frac{(1-\|\mathbf{W}_{1}\|_{2}\cdot\|\mathbf{W}_{2}\|_{2})r}{2} for some i∈{1,2}i\in\{1,2\}, where r=mini∈{1,2}⁡‖𝐲i‖2r=\min_{i\in\{1,2\}}\|\mathbf{y}_{i}\|_{2}.

Sketch of Proof.

Theorem 5.7 is stated using an exact matching constraint on each target output vector 𝐲i\mathbf{y}_{i}. However, the proof remains valid under a relaxed geometric condition: instead of requiring exact recovery, one may demand that the transformer output lies at distance at most r/2r/2 from each 𝐲i\mathbf{y}_{i}, where the 𝐲i\mathbf{y}_{i} are mutually orthogonal vectors in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} with norm greater than rr. Since these vectors form a high-dimensional orthogonal configuration, any point in the space that lies within r/2r/2 of hh of them must necessarily be at distance at least r/2r/2 from the remaining one. This relaxation preserves the essential conclusion: the set of simultaneously approximable outputs is confined to a strict subspace of the full output space. ∎

The full proof can be found in Appendix F.

6 Conclusion

This work advances the theoretical understanding of prompt tuning by analyzing the memorization capacity of transformer architectures. We established that the amount of information a transformer can reliably encode through prompt tuning is fundamentally limited as the number of input/output couples that can be memorized scales at most linearly with the prompt length. More importantly, we provided the first formal justification for the empirically observed degradation in transformer performance with long contexts. Our results demonstrate that transformers suffer from an intrinsic memory limitation, independent of context length. These findings highlight a fundamental limitation in the use of prompt tuning in transformer-based models.

Appendix A Proof of the Properties of Mean-Field Generalization

Let us prove that mean-field self-attention FF generalizes discrete self-attention Att\operatorname{Att} in the sense that for any input 𝐗∈ℝd×m\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times m}, we have F⁡(M⁡(𝐗))=M⁡(Att⁡(𝐗,𝐗))F(\mathrm{M}(\mathbf{X}))=\mathrm{M}(\operatorname{Att}(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{X})).

Proof.

Let 𝐗∈ℝd×m,𝐲∈ℝd\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times m},\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, Att\operatorname{Att} be the self-attention layer parameterized by projection matrices 𝐖q\mathbf{W}_{q}, 𝐖k\mathbf{W}_{k}, 𝐖v\mathbf{W}_{v}, and 𝐖o\mathbf{W}_{o} as defined in Definition 2.1, and FF be the mean-field generalization of Att\operatorname{Att}. Then

M⁡(Att⁡(𝐗,𝐗))\displaystyle\mathrm{M}\big(\operatorname{Att}(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{X})\big) =M([Att(𝐗:,1,𝐗),…,Att(𝐗:,m,𝐗)])\displaystyle=\mathrm{M}\big(\left[\operatorname{Att}(\mathbf{X}_{:,1},\mathbf{X}),\;\ldots,\;\operatorname{Att}(\mathbf{X}_{:,m},\mathbf{X})\right]\big)
=M⁡([𝐱l]l∈[m])\displaystyle=\mathrm{M}\Big([\mathbf{x}_{l}]_{l\in[m]}\Big)
=1m​∑l=1mδ𝐱l,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{l=1}^{m}\delta_{\mathbf{x}_{l}},

writing

𝐱l\displaystyle\mathbf{x}_{l} =∑i=1h𝐖oi​𝐖vi​𝐗⋅σ⁡((𝐖ki​𝐗)⊤​𝐖qi​𝐗l)\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{h}\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{o}}^{i}\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{v}}^{i}\mathbf{X}\cdot\sigma\big((\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{k}}^{i}\mathbf{X})^{\top}\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{q}}^{i}\mathbf{X}_{l}\big)
=∑i=1h∑j=1m𝐖oi​𝐖vi​𝐗j​exp⁡((𝐖ki​𝐗j)⊤​𝐖qi​𝐗l)∑j=1mexp⁡((𝐖ki​𝐗j)⊤​𝐖qi​𝐗l)\displaystyle=\sum_{i=1}^{h}\frac{\sum_{j=1}^{m}\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{o}}^{i}\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{v}}^{i}\mathbf{X}_{j}\exp\big((\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{k}}^{i}\mathbf{X}_{j})^{\top}\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{q}}^{i}\mathbf{X}_{l})}{\sum_{j=1}^{m}\exp\big((\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{k}}^{i}\mathbf{X}_{j})^{\top}\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{q}}^{i}\mathbf{X}_{l})}
=ΓM⁡(𝐗)​(𝐗l).\displaystyle=\Gamma_{\mathrm{M}(\mathbf{X})}(\mathbf{X}_{l}).

Hence

(M​(Att⁡(𝐗,𝐗)))​(𝐲)\displaystyle\Big(\mathrm{M}(\operatorname{Att}(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{X}))\Big)(\mathbf{y}) =1m​∑l=1m𝟏𝐱l=𝐲\displaystyle=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{l=1}^{m}\mathbf{1}_{\mathbf{x}_{l}=\mathbf{y}}
=1m​∑l=1m𝟏ΓM⁡(𝐗)​(𝐗l)=𝐲\displaystyle=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{l=1}^{m}\mathbf{1}_{\Gamma_{\mathrm{M}(\mathbf{X})}(\mathbf{X}_{l})=\mathbf{y}}
=1m​∑l=1m𝟏𝐗l∈ΓM⁡(𝐗)−1​(𝐲)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{l=1}^{m}\mathbf{1}_{\mathbf{X}_{l}\in\Gamma_{\mathrm{M}(\mathbf{X})}^{-1}(\mathbf{y})}
=M⁡(𝐗)​(ΓM⁡(𝐗)−1​(𝐲))\displaystyle=\mathrm{M}(\mathbf{X})\big(\Gamma_{\mathrm{M}(\mathbf{X})}^{-1}(\mathbf{y})\big)
=((ΓM⁡(𝐗))♯​M​(𝐗))​(𝐲)\displaystyle=\Big((\Gamma_{\mathrm{M}(\mathbf{X})})_{\sharp}{\mathrm{M}(\mathbf{X})}\Big)(\mathbf{y})
=(F​(M​(𝐗)))​(𝐲).\displaystyle=\Big(F\big(\mathrm{M}(\mathbf{X})\big)\Big)(\mathbf{y}).

∎

We use the same proof to show that a mean-field transformer layer TT generalizes a discrete transformer layer τ\tau in the sense that for any input 𝐗∈ℝd×m\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times m}, we have T⁡(M⁡(𝐗))=M⁡(τ⁡(𝐗))T(\mathrm{M}(\mathbf{X}))=\mathrm{M}(\tau(\mathbf{X})).

Proof.

Let 𝐗∈ℝd×m,𝐲∈ℝd\mathbf{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times m},\mathbf{y}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, τ\tau be a transformer layer with self-attention Att\operatorname{Att} as described above and MLP layer MLP\operatorname{MLP}, and FF be the mean-field generalization of Att\operatorname{Att}. Then

M⁡(τ⁡(𝐗))\displaystyle\mathrm{M}(\tau(\mathbf{X})) =M(MLP([Att(𝐗:,l,𝐗)]l∈[m])+𝐗)\displaystyle=\mathrm{M}\Big(\operatorname{MLP}\big([\operatorname{Att}(\mathbf{X}_{:,l},\mathbf{X})]_{l\in[m]}\big)+\mathbf{X}\Big)
=M⁡([𝐱l]l∈[m])\displaystyle=\mathrm{M}\Big([\mathbf{x}_{l}]_{l\in[m]}\Big)
=1m​∑l=1mδ𝐱l,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{l=1}^{m}\delta_{\mathbf{x}_{l}},

writing

𝐱l\displaystyle\mathbf{x}_{l} =MLP⁡(∑i=1h𝐖oi​𝐖vi​𝐗⋅σ⁡((𝐖ki​𝐗)⊤​𝐖qi​𝐗l))+𝐗l\displaystyle=\operatorname{MLP}\Big(\sum_{i=1}^{h}\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{o}}^{i}\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{v}}^{i}\mathbf{X}\cdot\sigma\big((\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{k}}^{i}\mathbf{X})^{\top}\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{q}}^{i}\mathbf{X}_{l}\big)\Big)+\mathbf{X}_{l}
=MLP⁡(∑i=1h∑j=1m𝐖oi​𝐖vi​𝐗j​exp⁡((𝐖ki​𝐗j)⊤​𝐖qi​𝐗l)∑j=1mexp⁡((𝐖ki​𝐗j)⊤​𝐖qi​𝐗l))+𝐗l\displaystyle=\operatorname{MLP}\Big(\sum_{i=1}^{h}\frac{\sum_{j=1}^{m}\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{o}}^{i}\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{v}}^{i}\mathbf{X}_{j}\exp\big((\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{k}}^{i}\mathbf{X}_{j})^{\top}\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{q}}^{i}\mathbf{X}_{l})}{\sum_{j=1}^{m}\exp\big((\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{k}}^{i}\mathbf{X}_{j})^{\top}\mathbf{W}_{\mathrm{q}}^{i}\mathbf{X}_{l})}\Big)+\mathbf{X}_{l}
=ΔM⁡(𝐗)​(𝐗l).\displaystyle=\Delta_{\mathrm{M}(\mathbf{X})}(\mathbf{X}_{l}).

Hence

(M​(τ​(𝐗)))​(𝐲)\displaystyle\Big(\mathrm{M}(\tau(\mathbf{X}))\Big)(\mathbf{y}) =1m​∑l=1m𝟏𝐱l=𝐲\displaystyle=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{l=1}^{m}\mathbf{1}_{\mathbf{x}_{l}=\mathbf{y}}
=1m​∑l=1m𝟏ΔM⁡(𝐗)​(𝐗l)=𝐲\displaystyle=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{l=1}^{m}\mathbf{1}_{\Delta_{\mathrm{M}(\mathbf{X})}(\mathbf{X}_{l})=\mathbf{y}}
=1m​∑l=1m𝟏𝐗l∈ΔM⁡(𝐗)−1​(𝐲)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{l=1}^{m}\mathbf{1}_{\mathbf{X}_{l}\in\Delta_{\mathrm{M}(\mathbf{X})}^{-1}(\mathbf{y})}
=M⁡(𝐗)​(ΔM⁡(𝐗)−1​(𝐲))\displaystyle=\mathrm{M}(\mathbf{X})\big(\Delta_{\mathrm{M}(\mathbf{X})}^{-1}(\mathbf{y})\big)
=((ΔM⁡(𝐗))♯​M​(𝐗))​(𝐲)\displaystyle=\Big((\Delta_{\mathrm{M}(\mathbf{X})})_{\sharp}{\mathrm{M}(\mathbf{X})}\Big)(\mathbf{y})
=(T​(M​(𝐗)))​(𝐲).\displaystyle=\Big(T\big(\mathrm{M}(\mathbf{X})\big)\Big)(\mathbf{y}).

∎

Appendix B Proof of the Lower Bounds for the Covering Number

We use the critical parameters introduced in Kloeckner [2012] to prove Proposition 3.6.

Lemma B.1.

Let (𝒳,d)(\mathcal{X},d) be a Polish space. If crit𝒫⁡(𝒳)>s\operatorname{crit}_{\mathcal{P}}(\mathcal{X})>s, then there exists a constant C>0C>0 such that 𝒩⁡(𝒳,d,ε)≥1C​exp⁡(1εs)\mathcal{N}(\mathcal{X},d,\varepsilon)\geq\frac{1}{C}\exp(\frac{1}{\varepsilon^{s}}).

Proof.

From Frostman’s Lemma [Kloeckner, 2014], we obtain a Borel probability measure μ\mu on 𝒳\mathcal{X} and a constant C>0C>0 such that

∀𝐱∈𝒳,∀r>0,μ⁡(B⁡(𝐱,r))≤C​exp⁡(−1rs).\forall\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{X},\forall r>0,\mu(B(\mathbf{x},r))\leq C\exp(-\frac{1}{r^{s}}).

Then, taking an ε\varepsilon-cover of 𝒳\mathcal{X}

𝒳⊂⋃i=1𝒩⁡(𝒳,d,ε)B⁡(xi,ε),\mathcal{X}\subset\bigcup_{i=1}^{\mathcal{N}(\mathcal{X},d,\varepsilon)}B(x_{i},\varepsilon),

we get

1\displaystyle 1 =μ⁡(𝒳)\displaystyle=\mu(\mathcal{X})
≤∑i=1𝒩⁡(𝒳,d,ε)μ⁡(B⁡(xi,ε))\displaystyle\leq\sum_{i=1}^{\mathcal{N}(\mathcal{X},d,\varepsilon)}\mu(B(x_{i},\varepsilon))
≤𝒩⁡(𝒳,d,ε)​C​exp⁡(−1εs).\displaystyle\leq\mathcal{N}(\mathcal{X},d,\varepsilon)C\exp(-\frac{1}{\varepsilon^{s}}).

Hence

𝒩⁡(𝒳,d,ε)≥1C​exp⁡(1εs).\mathcal{N}(\mathcal{X},d,\varepsilon)\geq\frac{1}{C}\exp(\frac{1}{\varepsilon^{s}}).

∎

Proof of Proposition 3.6.

Proposition 3.6 comes from the fact that (𝒢,Wq)(\mathcal{G},W_{q}) is a Polish space [Villani, 2008, Chapter 6] satisfying crit𝒫⁡(𝒢)≥d\operatorname{crit}_{\mathcal{P}}(\mathcal{G})\geq d [Kloeckner, 2014, Theorem 1.3]. ∎

Therefore, for m​k>mp​log⁡(3​L​r)−log⁡(ε)log⁡(r)−log⁡(3​ε)mk>m_{p}\frac{\log(3Lr)-\log(\varepsilon)}{\log(r)-\log(3\varepsilon)}, some output sequences aren’t ε\varepsilon-accessible by 𝐗\mathbf{X}, and the proportion of output sequences that are ε\varepsilon-accessible is at most CinCout\frac{C_{\mathrm{in}}}{C_{\mathrm{out}}}. ∎

Therefore, for k>(6​L​rε)d​(1+log⁡(1+(4​L​rε)q))(3ε)d−log⁡(C)k>\frac{(\frac{6Lr}{\varepsilon})^{d}(1+\log(1+(\frac{4Lr}{\varepsilon})^{q}))}{(\frac{3}{\varepsilon})^{d}-\log(C)}, some output distributions aren’t ε\varepsilon-accessible by 𝐗\mathbf{X}, and the proportion of output distributions that are ε\varepsilon-accessible is at most CinCout\frac{C_{\mathrm{in}}}{C_{\mathrm{out}}}. ∎

Appendix F Proof of Theorem 5.8

We provide the proof for h=1h=1 for clarity. First, let us generalize Lemma E.1 to the outcome "there is no 𝐏\mathbf{P} such that |𝐚i𝐏−𝐲i|<r2|\mathbf{a}_{i}^{\mathbf{P}}-\mathbf{y}_{i}|<\frac{r}{2} for all i∈{1,2}i\in\{1,2\}".
